title: Minimise Clipping Points by Removing One Element
statement:
You are given an array `a` of `n` integers. An element is a **clipping point** if it is an *internal* element (it has a neighbour on both sides) and it is **strictly greater** than both of its neighbours or **strictly smaller** than both of its neighbours. The first and last elements are never clipping points, and an element equal to a neighbour is not a clipping point.

You must remove **exactly one** element from the array. The remaining elements keep their relative order and become adjacent, so the neighbours of elements next to the removed one change.

Print the **minimum** number of clipping points the remaining array can have, over all choices of the element to remove.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` space-separated integers `a[0], ..., a[n-1]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum possible number of clipping points after removing one element.

examples.explanation: The clipping points of the original array are 5, 2 and 4. Removing 2 gives `1 5 4 3`, where only 5 is a clipping point. Removing any other element leaves at least one clipping point as well, so the minimum is 1.
Equal neighbours never make a clipping point, so the array has none and removing any element keeps it at 0.
The original array has four clipping points. Removing the `1` at index 2 gives `1 3 3 1 3`, where only the `1` at index 3 is strictly smaller than both neighbours. No removal reaches 0.

hints: Trying every removal and recounting from scratch costs O(n) each, O(n^2) overall. Which elements can change their clipping status when one element is removed?
Only the removed element and its two neighbours are affected. Every other element keeps the same neighbours as before.
Count the clipping points once. For each removal, subtract the original status of the (up to three) affected positions and add the status of the two neighbours using their new adjacent values.
